author: Mhdasm
description: The Mughal emperor Mirza Nasir al-Din Muhammad, popularly known as Humayun, is buried in Humayun's tomb (Persian: Maqbara-i Humayun), which is located in Delhi, India. Under the patronage of Empress Bega Begum, Humayun's first wife and primary consort, the mausoleum was commissioned in 1558 and constructed by Persian architects Mirak Mirza Ghiyas and his son Sayyid Muhammad. It is situated in Nizamuddin East, Delhi, near the Dina-panah Citadel, also known as Purana Qila (Old Fort), which Humayun discovered in 1538. It was the first garden-tomb on the Indian subcontinent. Additionally, it was the first building to use red sandstone on that big of a scale. Following its 1993 designation as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the tomb has undergone considerable restoration work, notably.

file: Courtyard and Mahabharata Reliefs at the Kailasa Temple, Ellora 01.jpg
author: Rohit Sharma
description: The Kailasa Temple at Ellora (Cave 16) is a remarkable example of rock-cut architecture, commissioned in the 8th century by Rashtrakuta king Krishna I. Carved entirely out of a single basalt rock, the temple represents a monolithic excavation rather than constructed assembly, making it one of the largest free-standing rock-cut structures in the world. Architecturally, it is designed as a multi-storeyed  complex with a central sanctum (garbhagriha) housing a Shiva lingam, surrounded by intricately sculpted mandapas, pillared halls, and sub-shrines. The temple exhibits precise spatial planning, with axial alignment, carved columns, and elaborately detailed reliefs depicting episodes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata, and Puranic traditions. Its technical brilliance lies in the sequential top-down excavation method, extensive use of structural relief, and integration of functional spaces (courtyards, stairways, and water channels) within a single rock mass, exemplifying the apex of early medieval Indian engineering and sculptural artistry.
